concepts.def: The mass of product that would be obtained if every one of the reactant particles reacted in the way the balanced equation shows and none of the product was lost. It is the largest mass that could possibly form, so it is the figure the actual mass is compared with.
The amount of a product obtained from a reaction. It is the amount actually made and collected, measured after the product has been separated from the reaction mixture.
The yield compared with the maximum theoretical amount, expressed as a percentage. It measures how much of the possible product was actually obtained in that particular preparation.

% Yield = (Mass of product actually made) / (Maximum theoretical mass of product) x 100. The mass actually made goes on the top and the maximum theoretical mass on the bottom, so the answer can never exceed 100%.

concepts.term: Reversible reaction as a reason for a lower yield
concepts.def: The reaction may not go to completion because it is reversible. Reactants are still present when the amounts stop changing, so less product forms than the equation predicts.

Some of the product may be lost when it is separated from the reaction mixture, for example crystals left on filter paper, solution left in a beaker, or solid left behind on transfer. The product still exists, but it is not weighed.
Some of the reactants may react in ways different to the expected reaction, forming products other than the one wanted. Those atoms are then unavailable for the desired product, so its yield falls.

concepts.term: Conservation of atoms and a yield below 100%
concepts.def: No atoms are gained or lost in a chemical reaction, yet the calculated amount of product is not always obtained. The atoms still exist, but some are in unreacted reactants, in a different product, or in product that was never collected.

A measure of the amount of starting materials that end up as useful products. It is worked out from the balanced equation, so it is a property of the reaction chosen rather than of how well the experiment was carried out.

It is important for sustainable development and for economic reasons to use reactions with high atom economy: less of the starting material ends up as waste that must be treated or disposed of, and less raw material is bought for each tonne of useful product.

(Relative formula mass of desired product from equation) / (Sum of relative formula masses of all reactants from equation) x 100. Both figures are read from the balanced equation, including the balancing numbers.

The desired product is the substance the reaction is being carried out to make; any other product is a by-product. Atom economy is always quoted for a stated desired product, so the same reaction has different atom economies depending on which product is wanted.

A number written in front of a formula multiplies the whole of that relative formula mass. In Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2 the desired product term is 2 x 56 = 112 and the reactant total is 160 + (3 x 28) = 244.

concepts.term: Theoretical mass from a balanced equation
concepts.def: Divide the given mass of reactant by its relative formula mass, use the balanced equation to convert to the amount of product, then multiply by the relative formula mass of the product. This gives the maximum theoretical mass of that product.

Where more than one reaction makes the same product, the pathway chosen is judged on data such as atom economy, yield, rate, the position of any equilibrium and the usefulness of the by-products, not on any single one of these figures alone.

concepts.term: Percentage yield compared with atom economy
concepts.def: Percentage yield measures how much of the possible product a particular preparation actually delivered. Atom economy measures how much of the starting material the equation itself sends into the desired product. A reaction can be high in one and low in the other.

A by-product that can be sold or used elsewhere means less of the starting material is truly wasted, so a pathway with a modest atom economy may still be chosen. The by-product does not change the atom economy figure for the desired product.

mcqs.q: A student calculates that 8.0 g of copper sulfate crystals should form, but obtains 6.2 g after filtering, washing and drying. Which statement best explains the shortfall?
options: Some atoms were destroyed as the reaction took place, so less product formed.
Mass is conserved only when the reaction is carried out in a sealed vessel.
Some of the product was left behind when it was separated from the mixture.
The relative formula mass used for the crystals must have been too large.
mcqs.explain: One of the three reasons the specification gives: product lost during separation is never weighed, so the actual yield falls below the theoretical maximum.

mcqs.q: An industrial reaction is written with a reversible arrow. Why does this reduce the yield of the product?
options: The reaction runs backwards instead, so no product is obtained at all.
The yield is fine if the mixture is simply left to run for much longer.
The product decomposes into substances that are not shown in the equation.
The reaction does not go to completion, so reactants remain at the end.
mcqs.explain: The specification's first reason: a reversible reaction may not go to completion, so some reactant is never converted.

mcqs.q: A student transfers a precipitate from the filter paper to a watch glass and some is left on the paper. What happens to the percentage yield?
options: It rises, because the maximum theoretical mass used becomes smaller.
It is unchanged, because no atoms can be lost in a chemical reaction.
It cannot be found until the precipitate left behind has been weighed.
It falls, because the mass of product actually made is now smaller.
mcqs.explain: The top of the equation is the mass actually obtained, so product left behind lowers it while the theoretical mass is unchanged.

mcqs.q: Methane burned in a limited supply of air produces some carbon monoxide as well as carbon dioxide. Why is the yield of carbon dioxide lower than expected?
options: Some of the reactants have reacted in a way different to the expected one.
Carbon atoms are lost from the system when carbon monoxide is formed.
The reaction is reversible, so carbon dioxide changes back into methane.
Carbon monoxide has a smaller relative formula mass than carbon dioxide.
mcqs.explain: The specification's third reason: atoms taken by a competing reaction cannot appear in the desired product.

mcqs.q: What does the percentage yield of a reaction compare?
options: The mass of product actually made with the maximum theoretical mass.
The mass of the desired product with the total mass of all reactants.
The maximum theoretical mass with the mass of product actually made.
The mass of the useful product with the mass of the waste products.
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's definition: the yield compared with the maximum theoretical amount, as a percentage.

mcqs.q: The maximum theoretical mass of magnesium oxide is 8.0 g. A student obtains 6.4 g. What is the percentage yield?
mcqs.explain: 6.4 / 8.0 x 100 = 80%, actual mass over maximum theoretical mass.

mcqs.q: A preparation has a maximum theoretical mass of 3.6 g. After filtering, 2.7 g of dry product is collected. What is the percentage yield?
CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Relative formula masses: CaCO3 = 100, CaO = 56. What is the maximum theoretical mass of calcium oxide from 25 g of calcium carbonate?
mcqs.explain: 25 / 100 = 0.25 mol CaCO3, giving 0.25 mol CaO, and 0.25 x 56 = 14 g.

mcqs.q: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. Ar(Mg) = 24, Mr(MgO) = 40. What is the maximum theoretical mass of magnesium oxide from 4.8 g of magnesium?
mcqs.explain: 4.8 / 24 = 0.2 mol Mg, and the 2 : 2 ratio gives 0.2 mol MgO, so 0.2 x 40 = 8.0 g.

mcqs.q: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. Mr(Fe2O3) = 160, Ar(Fe) = 56. What is the maximum theoretical mass of iron from 320 g of iron(III) oxide?
mcqs.explain: 320 / 160 = 2 mol Fe2O3, which gives 4 mol Fe, and 4 x 56 = 224 g.

mcqs.q: What does the atom economy of a reaction measure?
options: The amount of the theoretical product that is obtained in practice.
The amount of the starting materials that ends up as useful products.
How carefully the product was separated from the reaction mixture.
The share of the atoms in the product taken from the main reactant.
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's definition of atom economy, also called atom utilisation.

mcqs.q: Why is it important to use reactions with a high atom economy?
options: The percentage yield of the reaction is then certain to be high as well.
It shows that the product has been separated without any loss occurring.
It means the reaction will reach completion much more quickly than others.
Less starting material is wasted, which matters for cost and sustainability.
mcqs.explain: The specification gives both reasons: high atom economy matters for sustainable development and for economic reasons.

mcqs.q: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Relative formula masses: CaCO3 = 100, CaO = 56, CO2 = 44. What is the atom economy for producing calcium oxide?
mcqs.explain: 56 / 100 x 100 = 56%: the relative formula mass of the desired product over the total for the reactants.

mcqs.q: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. Mr(Fe2O3) = 160, Mr(CO) = 28, Ar(Fe) = 56. What is the atom economy for producing iron?
What goes on the bottom line of a percentage atom economy calculation?
options: The relative formula mass of the reactant containing the desired product.
The relative formula masses of all the reactants shown in the equation.
The relative formula masses of the reactants without the balancing numbers.
The total mass of the reactants that was weighed out for the experiment.
mcqs.explain: The specification's equation uses the sum of the relative formula masses of all reactants from the equation.

mcqs.q: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2. Ar(Zn) = 65, Mr(H2SO4) = 98, Mr(H2) = 2. What is the atom economy for producing hydrogen?
Two pathways make the same product. Pathway 1: atom economy 100%, yield 95%, fast. Pathway 2: atom economy 55%, yield 95%, fast, by-product sold as fertiliser. Which choice is better justified?
options: Pathway 1, because the same product is made from less starting material.
Pathway 2, because selling a by-product always outweighs a lower economy.
Pathway 2, because a lower atom economy gives it the higher percentage yield.
Pathway 1, because a 100% atom economy also guarantees that no product is lost.
mcqs.explain: With yield and rate matched, the higher atom economy means less raw material is bought and less waste is made.

mcqs.q: Pathway A: atom economy 90%, reversible, reaches equilibrium at 12% yield, very slow. Pathway B: atom economy 60%, yield 90%, fast, by-product is useful. Why might B be chosen?
options: A has to be chosen, because atom economy is the measure that decides.
A is not possible at all, because a reversible reaction makes no product.
B makes far more product per day and its by-product is still used.
B is better because 60% atom economy means the product is 60% pure.
mcqs.explain: Weighs rate, yield, equilibrium position and usefulness of by-products against A's higher atom economy, as the specification requires.

mcqs.q: N2 + 3H2 gives 2NH3 in a reversible reaction. Mr values: N2 = 28, H2 = 2, NH3 = 17. The atom economy is 100% but the percentage yield is low. Why?
options: Every reactant atom can reach the ammonia, but the reaction is incomplete.
A 100% atom economy means the low percentage yield must be a measuring error.
Atom economy and percentage yield are the same, so one figure has to be wrong.
Ammonia escapes as a gas, so the true atom economy is well below 100%.
mcqs.explain: 34 / 34 x 100 = 100% atom economy, while reversibility stops the reaction going to completion, so the yield is lower.

mcqs.q: In which reaction is the atom economy for the named product 100%?
options: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2, making calcium oxide
C2H4 + H2O -> C2H5OH, making ethanol
2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2, making oxygen
Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu, making copper
mcqs.explain: There is only one product, so all the reactant mass, 28 + 18 = 46, appears in the ethanol, Mr 46.
